   The History of the Printing Press: Revolutionizing Knowledge, Society, and Human Consciousness

  1. Introduction: The Pre-Gutenberg World and the Scarcity of the Written Word

  For the vast majority of human history, the preservation and dissemination of knowledge was an excruciatingly laborious, fragile, and elitist enterprise.
  Before the invention of mechanical movable type in mid-fifteenth-century Europe, the written word was governed by scribal culture. In medieval
  scriptoria—primarily situated within monasteries, cathedral schools, and later, the burgeoning university guilds—every individual manuscript was copied by
  hand. Scribes worked with quills and ink on parchment (prepared animal skins such as vellum) or, increasingly toward the end of the Middle Ages, rag-based
  paper.

  This manual method of text transmission suffered from three profound limitations: time, expense, and inaccuracy. To produce a single illuminated manuscript
  of the Latin Vulgate Bible or a treatise by Aristotle, a skilled scribe might labor for anywhere from six months to several years. The materials alone were
  prohibitively costly; producing a single substantial folio volume on vellum often required the hides of dozens or even hundreds of calves or sheep.
  Consequently, books were luxury goods, prized possessions held almost exclusively by ecclesiastical institutions, monarchies, and the wealthiest feudal
  nobility. A modest monastic library might consider itself well-stocked with a few hundred codices, many of which were literally chained to desks or
  lecterns to prevent theft.

  Moreover, hand-copying was inherently vulnerable to human error. With each successive generation of copies, transcription mistakes, misreadings, marginal
  glosses mistakenly integrated into the main text, and omissions compounded exponentially. A text copied in Bologna could deviate substantially from a
  version of the same title copied in Paris or Oxford. Knowledge was precarious, easily lost to fires, mold, war, or scribal carelessness. While oral culture
  remained the dominant mode of communication for over ninety percent of the population, literate culture was preserved in amber—static, highly centralized,
  and fiercely guarded by gatekeepers of religious orthodoxy and political authority.

  It was against this background of intellectual bottleneck and explosive demand for texts—driven by Renaissance humanism, urbanization, and the expansion of
  universities—that mechanical printing emerged, permanently transforming the trajectory of human civilization.
  ──────
  2. Antecedents and Global Origins: East Asian Innovations

  While Western historiography has long credited Johannes Gutenberg with inventing the printing press, the fundamental principles of printing—both block
  printing (xylography) and movable type—originated in East Asia centuries before European experiments began.

  Woodblock Printing in China and Korea

  Woodblock printing, where an entire page of text or illustration was carved in relief onto a block of wood, inked, and impressed onto paper or silk, was
  practiced in China as early as the Sui and Tang Dynasties (seventh and eighth centuries CE). Among the earliest surviving dated printed works in the world
  is the Chinese translation of the Diamond Sutra, printed in 868 CE during the Tang Dynasty. This scroll, discovered in the Mogao Caves at Dunhuang,
  demonstrates an astonishingly high level of technical mastery, typographic balance, and aesthetic maturity.

  Woodblock printing spread rapidly across East Asia. In Korea, the Mugujeonggwang Daedaranigyeong (The Great Dharani Sutra of Immaculate and Pure Light),
  discovered inside the Shakyamuni Pagoda of Bulguksa Temple, dates back to the first half of the eighth century (before 751 CE),
